children.text: Not every component of a transformation should be managed the same way. Some have a fixed legal deadline and a well-defined deliverable; a detailed plan, followed carefully, is exactly right for them. Others are trying to hit a target that is still moving, where the best plan is a short cycle of building, testing and adjusting. Managing both kinds identically guarantees that one of them is managed badly.

Chapter 15 assigns each of Vermont's components to a predictive, adaptive or hybrid approach. This lesson explains the three approaches as PMI's guidance describes them, shows how the book classifies the components and why, and sets out how a portfolio office governs a portfolio that mixes all three.
The choice is not a matter of fashion. It follows from two properties of each component: how stable its requirements are, and how much is gained by learning quickly from early results.
Three Approaches

A predictive approach, often called waterfall, defines scope, schedule and cost early and manages change through formal control. It suits work whose requirements are well understood and whose deadline is fixed. An adaptive approach, which includes agile methods, plans in short cycles, delivers in increments and expects requirements to change as the team learns. It suits work whose requirements cannot be fully known in advance.

Between them lies the hybrid approach: a component with fixed deliverables at its boundary and adaptive work inside it, or a mostly predictive plan with some agile elements. PMI's Agile Practice Guide, developed with the Agile Alliance and published in 2017, treats hybrid life cycles as a legitimate fit-for-purpose choice rather than a compromise, and describes combinations ranging from predominantly predictive with some agile components to largely agile with a predictive component.

PMI's recent standards have moved further in the same direction. The PMBOK Guide's eighth edition presents its process guidance as reference material that applies to predictive, agile and hybrid work alike. The choice of approach is now treated as one of the first decisions in managing any piece of work, not a matter of organizational style.

body.title: Choosing an approach

children.text: How Chapter 15 Classifies Vermont's Components

The book assigns predictive management to components with fixed statutory deadlines and well-defined deliverables: the reference-based-pricing methodology rulemaking, the Statewide Strategic Plan (with adaptive elements), the analytics-vendor deployment, Certified Community Behavioral Health Clinic certification, and AHS restructuring. Each has a defined end product and a date that cannot move.

Adaptive management goes to components where requirements evolve and rapid learning beats adherence to a fixed plan. The statewide AI-governance framework is the clearest case, because the regulatory landscape is changing faster than any fixed plan could anticipate. The Care Integration Network build-out depends on vendor outputs and an evolving FHIR ecosystem. Blueprint medical-home expansion proceeds practice by practice. And the HEROI equity-scoring methodology iterates as data quality improves.

The fourteen-hospital transformation planning effort is the book's hybrid example: fixed deliverables, because each hospital's plan is due on a schedule, with hospital-specific content developed iteratively inside that frame.

children.text: Why the Distinction Matters for the Portfolio

Using the wrong approach fails in predictable ways. Managing an adaptive component predictively produces a detailed plan that is out of date before it is approved, followed by a series of change requests that consume more effort than the work. Managing a predictive component adaptively risks missing a statutory deliverable while the team iterates on details that were never in question.

For the portfolio office, the approach also determines what progress looks like. A predictive component reports against its baseline: activities done, milestones met, earned value. An adaptive component reports learning and increments delivered: what was built this cycle, what was tested, what changed in the plan as a result. Holding an adaptive component to a baseline it was never meant to have will show it as permanently late; holding a predictive component only to increments will hide a slipping legal deadline.

The approach also interacts with the dependency logic from Lesson 7. Adaptive components upstream of a gate are especially important to watch, because their finish date is less certain by design. The Care Integration Network is adaptive and sits in the Technology pillar that gates Economics. A portfolio manager should track its increments closely, because the gate opens when enough of the network is genuinely usable, not when a planned date arrives.

Hybrid components need the most care, because they carry both risks. The fourteen hospital plans have fixed due dates, so the portfolio office must track them predictively at the boundary. Inside each plan, content is developed iteratively with each hospital, so the office should expect revisions and judge each plan by whether it is converging on a usable result rather than by whether it matches an early draft.

body.analogy: Building a bridge and designing a new clinical workflow are both projects, but nobody would manage them the same way. The bridge needs a complete design before the first pour, because changing it halfway is ruinous. The workflow is best tried with a few clinicians, adjusted and tried again, because no one can predict in advance how it will feel at 3 a.m. on a busy unit.

children.text: Governing a Mixed Portfolio

A portfolio that mixes approaches needs governance that respects both. The book's roadmap sets a fixed cadence for the whole portfolio: monthly governance reviews, quarterly performance reviews against the Vermont Scorecard, and annual portfolio rebalancing. Within that cadence, predictive components are reviewed against their baselines and stage gates, and adaptive components against their cycle outputs and the outcomes they are aiming at.

Two practices make the mix workable. First, every component, whatever its approach, states the outcome it exists to produce and the date by which the portfolio needs it, so adaptive work cannot drift indefinitely. Second, adaptive components declare in advance what evidence will show they are ready to open the next gate, so the decision is made on agreed criteria rather than on a plan date or a mood.

The book's credential mapping follows from the same distinction: PMP for the predictive components, PMI-ACP for the adaptive ones, which is why it recommends both for the Policy and Technology program managers whose pillars contain both kinds of work.

children.text: Classify Your Own Components

Take the inventory from Lesson 3 and add an approach column. For each component ask two questions: are its requirements stable enough to plan in detail now, and is there a fixed external deadline for a defined deliverable? Two yes answers point to predictive management. Two no answers point to adaptive. Mixed answers usually point to hybrid: fixed boundaries with iterative content inside them.

Then check your staffing against the classification. Teams experienced only in predictive delivery often struggle with adaptive components and vice versa. Where a pillar contains both, its program lead needs fluency in both, which is the logic behind the book's dual-credential recommendation for Policy and Technology.

Finally, check your reporting. If every component reports the same metrics in the same format, the portfolio office is probably holding some components to the wrong measure. Adjusting the report template to the approach is a small change that removes a large source of false alarms and false comfort.
A component reported as permanently late may simply be adaptive work held to a predictive baseline. Check the approach before you check the team.

points: Predictive management suits stable requirements and fixed deadlines; adaptive management suits evolving requirements and fast learning; hybrid combines fixed boundaries with iterative content.
PMI's Agile Practice Guide, developed with the Agile Alliance in 2017, treats hybrid life cycles as a legitimate fit-for-purpose choice.
Chapter 15 manages rulemaking, the Strategic Plan, the analytics deployment, CCBHC certification and AHS restructuring predictively.
The AI-governance framework, CIN build-out, Blueprint expansion and HEROI methodology are adaptive; the 14-hospital planning effort is hybrid.
The wrong approach fails predictably: stale plans and change-request overload, or missed legal deadlines.
A mixed portfolio shares one governance cadence but reports each component on the measure that fits its approach, with need-by dates and agreed gate evidence.
The book maps PMP to predictive work and PMI-ACP to adaptive work, which is why Policy and Technology leads need both.

body.explanation: The book classifies the AI-governance framework as adaptive because the regulatory landscape evolves faster than any fixed plan. Reporting it against a detailed predictive baseline will show it as permanently late regardless of progress. It should report cycle outputs against its outcome and need-by date, with agreed evidence for readiness.
